turn_text: Well Congressman Garaminde, you talked about your background in agriculture and also I've noted you were in the Peace Corps and you've implemented government programs and you've managed federal lands and probably the shortest term thing you've done has been in Washington. So I have to ask you somewhat tongue-in-cheek has no one told you you can't gain public support for building lakes and reservoirs anymore?

Well it's nothing quite like a drought to wake people up. We have not built reservoirs in California for 50 years. There are some that are very, very controversial and remain that way today, but there are some that my Republican colleague, Doug Lemauff, and I have introduced Site's Reservoir, which is off-stream. It's in a valley off of the main rivers. It's just a little creek that runs through this particular valley. So that one does not have the kind of environmental concerns that on-stream reservoirs have We do have a major reservoir, in fact, the largest Shasta Reservoir, which can be raised. There are some environmental issues because some streams will be flooded. But those are minor compared to the necessity of providing additional water. But the biggest reservoir of all in California, the two biggest reservoirs are the Snowpack and the CRS. There's little we can do about that. We're seeing a diminution in that as a result of warmer climate. And the second big reservoir are the underground aquifers. And so as we look to the future, we really must engage in what we call conjunctive water management. When there is surface water, when the rains are there and the snows in the mountains, we use that water for the immediate irrigation. And then we also use that water to replenish the underground aquifers. In some cases, those are injection wells. In some cases, they're suddenly basing but we have to do that so that those aquifers are there and those reservoirs surface reservoirs and the underground aquifers are there for the inevitable drought which occurs about once every seven to ten years. So we'll get past this one badly because we really didn't prepare for the drought. Hopefully the next time we will have enough sense as a result of this drought to put in place those storage reservoirs.

turn_text: Are you going to have to use imminent domain to be able to take that land? And if you build those reservoirs, will you only be able to use them for water supply?

No. All the reservoirs in California are multi-purpose reservoirs, including the off-stream reservoir site. There will certainly be a recreation reservoir. I think a significant portion of that reservoir should always be held and reserved for the next drought. And it will be an annual supply. There's some 600,000 acre feet of annual supply that could come out of the site's reservoir. Similarly with the others, would there be eminent domain absolutely in the case of sites? In the case of some of these other reservoirs, it's already public land in the river canyons. With regard to the underground aquifers, California does not have any state law regulating underground aquifers. That's coming. It will happen. Not soon, I suspect, but we're going to have to deal with the fact that we really will need in the future to provide some sort of regulation of these aquifers if we're ever going to be able to restore them. So these are complex issues, but the issues that the state has dealt with in some places very badly. In some places, well, Southern California, 25 years ago, had 300,000 acre feet of storage. Now they have over 3 million acre feet of storage, and those reservoirs and storage systems are rather full. But in the long term, there are other things we need to do beyond storage. The fifth biggest river on the west coast of the Western Hemisphere are the sanitation plants in Southern California. They're taking water from Northern California, from the Colorado pumping at 200, 500 miles, cleaning it, use it once, clean it to a higher standard than the day it arrives in Southern California. and they dump it in the ocean. That's rather foolish. So recycling in the next five years, you can generate over 500,000 acre feet of new water in Southern California simply by recycling the water that's already there. Some similarly in Northern California, again, conservation is big. turn_text: Do you in conclusion see that agriculture is always going to have a challenge of being able to get enough water to grow the crops we traditionally expect from California? And do you see that potentially that will make it in decline in number of acres if not in profitability in your state in the future?

Agriculture will remain a major and very, very important industry in California. There's always changes. Just if you observe agriculture over even a 10-year period, you'll see some crops going in, other crops coming out. And that's just the way it is, often propelled by market forces. Clearly, the water issue is going to change the cropping patterns in some areas. Some water districts have moved to permanent orchard crops that require far more water than the annual crops that were previously raised there, cotton or grains of various kinds. So in those areas where they do not have a guaranteed annual water supply, I suspect some of those orchards are going to go back into annual crops. But their market forces will also cause change to occur, as it always has. Labor market is a major issue, as seen in California. Orchards that require a large amount of labor, for example, the citrus or the stone fruit industry. You'll see those orchards going out and low labor intensive crops going in. So there are many, many forces at play. Water being one of them, all of that will over time cause a change in agriculture. Nevertheless, California is blessed with an extraordinary climate, very rich soils, and a lot of water. We need to use it well. We need to conserve. We need to be wise about where we're using it and how we use it. And we always must prepare for the inevitable drought.
